messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] distance 7 for density studies of birds
parts:
Mirium and Haris (list)

The submission of your two questions within an hour of each other leads me to suspect the two questions might be related, so I will deal with them in the same response.

These questions remind us of the rule that we cannot do a proper analysis without considering the survey design.  We do not know how many transects were sampled (output below suggests 11), nor the number of visits made per year.  Without those details, precise advice about analysis will be difficult to give.

Fortunately Mirium provided her data in the form of a spreadsheet.  From the transect label data, it appears in her situation there are 4 locations, three locations having 14 transects, the other having 11 transects.  It also appears that the transects were visited multiple times each year over the period 2009-2012.  She has also recorded species, cluster size, perpendicular distance, and a few other things.

The main cause of perceived over-estimation of density is failure to properly describe survey effort.  Mirium's spreadsheet shows all the detections.  What it does not show are visits to transects where no birds were seen.  For distance sampling, emphasis is upon sampling effort rather than the detections (of course the detections are important).

To produce reasonable estimates of density, a fundamental quantity needed is encounter rate (number of detections per unit of effort).  If the effort is mis-specified, then encounter rate will be wrong; specifically, if survey effort is specified as too small (not accounting for transect visits when no detections were made), then encounter rate will be improperly large, and consequently the estimate of density will be too large.

To organise your data in such a way that Distance can make sense of your survey design, I recommend the following.  There are more clever ways of doing this, but this might be the most simple.

Create 16 strata from your data: one for each location x year combination; e.g. Anam09 ... Anam12, Nell09 ... Nell12, Para09 ... Para12, Vaz09 ... Vaz12

Within each strata, list all 14 (or 11 transects); in the effort (or line length) field, multiply line length (1km) by the number of visits in the given year.  There will be a row in your datasheet for each sighting in that location x year combination indicating the transect on which the sighting was made.  Should there have been a transect on which there were no sightings on any visit, that transect (and its total length) must be present with the perpendicular distance column BLANK (to properly account for survey effort expended).

Use a data filter to use only the data for species 1 (GHB), then in your analysis, request a stratified estimate, resulting in 16 estimates; one for each location x year combination.  Repeat for the next species (MGH).  Note that species MPH was inly sighted in your fourth location (Vazhachal-shola) and there were only 42 detections, making fitting a detection function troublesome.

Finally, note that your perpendicular distance data will be problematic for producing suitable fits of detection functions (see histograms below).  My belief is that your hornbills were detecting you before you detected them and they were creeping away from the transect prior to detection.  I say this because for each location (pooled across years and species) there is a distinct lack of detections at distances <5m from the transect.  Conventional distance sampling assumes detection of all hornbills on the transect and a smooth declining number of detections as perpendicular distance increases.  Hence, fitting a half-normal detection function to these data may be the appropriate thing to do, but goodness of fit statistics will suggest the model does not fit.
